title: Clarence Williams, Buddy Bolden and Louis Armstrong's style
summary: La Rocca argues Clarence Williams could not have heard Bolden play, given dates he cites, and says Armstrong's style came from the Original Dixieland Jazz Band records.

blocks.x: Before who was this came to be?

I mean Clarence Williams. You got me right that time because I'm making a mistake. I'm just telling you, I'm reading. I'm not reading. I'm telling you from my mind. Clarence Williams came to New York around 1923. The first white man he met on Broadway was me with an introduction from A.J. Perron, which you'll find in their books too. And this Negro is supposed to have her buddy bowling play. Now let me tell you about this man, who he is, where he come from. If any of you serious scholars doubt me, I was just speaking about Clarence Williams when he came to New York. Now if any of you serious scholars doubt what I say, you look up the history of Clarence Williams. He was supposed to have heard Buddy Bowling play. Buddy Bowling, according to the statistics given out by the New Orleans Jazz Club, was incarcerated in the Crazy House. That's Jackson, Louisiana. In 1906. He was put in jail and held there a year before they put him in the Crazy House. That was 1906. This would make Clarence Williams about six years old or seven. Because at the age of eight years old, he lived with his grandmother in an alley in Plaquemine, Louisiana, where he was a shoeshine boy from a gentleman by the name of Ferdinand, H-E-R-B-E-R-T, Herbert, who ran a barber shop in the city of Plaquemine. Now this Negro didn't come to New Orleans to his late teens. He could have never heard Buddy Bowling play. This same thing applies to Little Louie. Little Louie heard the records of the original Dixieland Jazz Band, but I can tell you he never heard Bowling play. Stop the machine on me. Wait now. Little Louie, the man I'm talking about is Louis Armstrong, who's style is playing off the ostrich walk. If you serious scholars get down and listen to his record, Sweet Little Papa or Little Pa, you'll see what Little Rock is talking about. I want you to read a letter from Mr. Fowler. Just that paragraph where it comes in and talks about Louie's young life in New Orleans.
